why: Count what one chart carries: 27 logged readings, 5 labelled stops, 3 gridlines, 6 time ticks, a four-step gas strip with its own percentages and a live time and temperature readout, and see that the single function paint(p) moves the drawn line, the dot, the readout, the filled stops and the lit log row, so one number holds every state.

Notice that each of the 34 indexed rows has a one-line answer and a hand-written synonym string, ranking is three tiers (title start, title contains, synonym) above plain mentions, and the empty state gives the bar's phone number, which is why this answers questions where a plain search box only filters a list.

Notice that all 16 items get a name, a tabular price and a sentence specific to this shop, hierarchy comes only from an 8px red bar and a 44px uppercase group heading, and the rule style carries data, with 6 dashed rows meaning until it runs out, explained by a two-line key in the side column.

Notice that each of the 3 figures is followed by the sum behind it and the sums agree with each other, the unit drops from 64px to 22px beside the figure, and margin-top:auto separates number from claim, so a simple three-tile row reads as a ledger rather than as marketing stats.

Notice that the columns are hours, address and page links instead of link farms: 7 hour rows with today's row lifted by a script using the shop's timezone, one holiday exception, tel and mailto links, a 236px mark filling the label column, and a signup with one success line and two different error lines.
